title: Capacity Allocation at the Source: Sparse Target Optimization for LLM Knowledge Editing
claim: The method builds a target hidden state upstream via gradient descent, then edits a layer's parameters downstream to reach the desired output.
layout: 3 stacked rows, left-to-right flow, gradient-descent arrow looping down between rows
description: A three-row block diagram of locate-then-edit model editing. The top row runs left to right: an Inputs box, then h0, then a light-blue m0 box labeled as the decisive Layer l, then h_L, ending in the loss H(Ŷ, Y target). A long arrow from the loss goes down and back left, labeled step 1 Gradient descent, into an orange box m in the middle row. A second arrow, step 2 Edit Layer l, drops from m to the bottom row. The bottom row repeats the same chain (Inputs, h0, the orange edited m at Layer l', h'_{L-1}, h'_L) and ends in Y target. Colors mark decisive (blue) and edited (orange) states. Layer labels sit above the arrows in italic serif and math notation. The eye goes first to the top row and then follows the numbered arrows.
caption: Overview of locate-then-edit model editing. The method first finds a target hidden state for the decisive token at the decisive layer via gradient descent (we call it upstream target construction), then edits a key subset of parameters to steer the original hidden state (m0) toward this target (m), producing the desired output (Ytarget) (we call it downstream parameter updating).
abstract: Knowledge editing has emerged as a promising approach for efficiently updating embedded knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It first computes an ideal target hidden state that steers the LLM toward the new output, and then edits the model parameters so that the original hidden state is mapped to this target. While most existing methods focus on the second stage of parameter editing in preserving other knowledge, we find that the upstream construction of the target hidden state also plays an important role in allocating the model's limited capacity space. We first establish a theoretical connection between interference in the parameter space and interference between target hidden states, showing that the two are positively correlated. Building on this insight, we propose a simple yet effective $\ell_1$ regularization method that prunes away unnecessary ``tentacles'' of each knowledge vector, retaining only the essential components. With fewer extraneous tentacles, each edit affects less other knowledge, enabling better coexistence. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of our method. Code: https://github.com/wintersdragon-c/STO.
